text:
Education in Sweden is structured into a nine-year compulsory comprehensive school (grundskola) from ages 6 to 16, followed by a three-year upper secondary school (gymnasieskola) from ages 16 to 19. The primary school curriculum includes Swedish, mathematics, physical education, English, handicrafts, music, visual arts, technology, physics, chemistry, biology, history, social studies, religion, and geography. Students receive grades from year 6, with a system using A–F, where A is the highest and F is failing. A total score, calculated from subject grades, determines eligibility for upper secondary school. National tests are administered in grades 3, 6, and 9, assessing students in core subjects.
Upper secondary education offers 18 national programs, including preparatory and vocational tracks, with a focus on theoretical subjects. All students complete a diploma project, which is not included in their merit score. Admission to upper secondary school is based on grades from compulsory school, with some programs requiring entrance exams. Higher education includes public universities and university colleges offering bachelor’s, master’s, and doctoral degrees, with the Bologna Process standardizing qualifications. The grading system varies by institution, using systems such as A–F, VG/G/U, or pass/fail.
Preschool is free and accessible to all children from age one, with at least three hours of daily education. Independent schools (friskolor) are publicly funded and offer diverse pedagogical approaches, though they have faced criticism over educational standards and profit-making. The education system emphasizes equality, inclusion, and quality, with strong support for special education and anti-discrimination policies. PISA and PIRLS results show strong performance in reading and mathematics, though recent reports have highlighted concerns over declining test scores and the impact of immigration.
